summary: This informational report records the conclusions of an IAB workshop on character sets held in early 1996. It explains why Internet protocols that carry text need character set handling, recommends tagging text using MIME, recommends a default character set, and makes recommendations to the IAB, IANA and the IESG.

eli5.summary: Different people write with different alphabets, so this report says how to label which one a message uses.

questions: how should internet protocols handle character sets
what is a coded character set

why is utf-8 the default for new protocols
how should text be labeled with its charset
subtitle: An IAB workshop's answer to a messy question: how should Internet protocols say which alphabet and encoding a piece of text uses?

tldr.problem: The term 'character set' means different things to different people, and mail, directories and the Web each handle the many text encodings in their own way.
tldr.mechanism: The workshop proposed a layered model in which a Coded Character Set, a Character Encoding Scheme and a Transfer Encoding Syntax are labeled explicitly, preferably with MIME tags, and recommended ISO 10646 and UTF-8 as defaults for new protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational report, not a standard, and the defaults do not deprecate other character sets. It has since been updated by RFC 6055.

facts.label: Default encoding for new text protocols

today: RFC 2130 is an Informational report and has been updated by RFC 6055. It records workshop recommendations and does not specify a standard.

sections.title: The Character Set Problem
sections.content:
RFC 2130 reports on an IAB-sponsored invitational workshop held 29 February to 1 March 1996 at the Information Sciences Institute in Marina del Rey, California. Its goal was to give the IAB and the IETF guidance on character sets and, if possible, a common framework for interoperability.

The trouble starts with the words. 'Character set' is used for many things, and even the MIME registry of character sets contains items whose meaning and use differ greatly. There is also a vast profusion of text encodings, which the report says is not itself a problem because each evolved for a real need. The problem is that mail, directories and the World Wide Web each developed different techniques for handling them.

The workshop declared several topics out of scope, including glyphs, sorting, user interface issues, fonts, locale in the POSIX sense and Han unification issues. A guiding concern was that the framework must not break existing protocols.
sections.eli5: Imagine every kid in a class writing notes in a different secret code, and nobody saying which one. The workshop wanted a simple way to say which code a note uses.

sections.title: The Architectural Model
sections.content:
The report splits text handling into seven layers. Four concern presenting text to a person: layout, culture, locale and language. Three are needed for text to go across the wire, and each should be explicitly specified by the sender (with the occasional exception of language):

  • The Coded Character Set (CCS) is a mapping from a set of abstract characters to a set of integers. Examples: ISO 10646, US-ASCII and the ISO-8859 series.
  • The Character Encoding Scheme (CES) is a mapping from one or several coded character sets to a set of octets. Examples: ISO 2022 and UTF-8. UTF-8 applies only to ISO 10646.
  • The Transfer Encoding Syntax (TES) is a transformation applied so the encoded text can be transmitted. Examples: Base64 and gzip.

In MIME, the charset parameter of the Content-Type header field specifies the CCS and CES together, and Content-Transfer-Encoding specifies the TES. The report notes that a MIME charset cuts across several layers and recommends that the MIME registration procedure for character sets show how a proposed character set deals with the CCS and the CES.
sections.eli5: Sending text is like mailing a letter. First you choose the alphabet, then how the letters become bytes, then how to wrap the package for the post. Each step needs to be written on the label.

sections.title: Labeling Text and Choosing Defaults
sections.content:
There are six ways a receiver can learn which CCS, CES and TES are in use: by guessing, by the standard that defines the protocol, by a label attached to the transfer envelope, by information inside the data stream, by prior bilateral agreement, or by negotiation during protocol start-up. The report calls guessing obviously not foolproof. It recommends that MIME-registered values be used for all tagging of character sets and languages unless an existing mechanism, other than guessing, already provides the information.

It does not set one mandatory default for all protocols, but it does recommend some. The default CCS is the repertoire of ISO 10646. For text-oriented protocols, new protocols should use UTF-8 as the CES, while protocols with a backwards-compatibility requirement should keep the existing default, such as US-ASCII for mail and ISO-8859-1 for HTTP. There is no recommended default for the transport encoding or for the language level, and the default locale is the POSIX locale.

Each protocol should clearly state what it uses for every layer, and clients should never have to guess. Stored text should be tagged in a MIME-compliant way so it can still be interpreted later. The defaults do not deprecate other character sets; they are guidance for interoperability.
sections.eli5: Always put a label on the text. If nobody has chosen another label, the report suggests the big shared alphabet, ISO 10646, written in UTF-8, because it still lets plain old English letters go through as they are.

sections.title: Converting Between Character Sets
sections.content:
The report gives guidelines for converting a source text S in one coded character set to a target text T in another. If the repertoire of the source is equal to or a subset of the target's, exact conversion is possible and the octets only need to be remapped.

In all other cases the conversion creates a text that differs from the original, and the choice among approaches depends on the purpose. A length-modifying conversion for human display turns one source character into one or several target characters by best resemblance, for example a copyright sign becoming (c). A length-preserving conversion maps each source character to exactly one target character. A conversion without data loss must be completely reversible, typically for storage, and needs an escape-style mapping, which the report notes effectively adds another level of encoding on top of the target. The client application should, where possible, be told what was done to the text.
sections.eli5: If a friend's alphabet has a letter yours lacks, you can write it as a few letters, swap in the closest one, or use a secret code so you can change it back later.

sections.title: Open Issues: Languages, Identifiers and Han
sections.content:
Three problems kept coming up and were left for other forums. The first is language tags and the 'CJK issue': Han unification uses one ISO 10646 code point for several national variants of a Chinese character, so an application cannot pick the right variant without more information. The workshop agreed language tags would be sufficient to disambiguate and recommended the MIME Content-Language header, while listing open questions about whether it is suitable. It also recommended that support for language tagging should be built into new protocols.

The second is public identifiers. There is considerable demand for non-ASCII characters in URL names, IMAP mailbox names and file names, and the report calls this still an open problem. For identifiers, it quotes RFC 1958 on public names being case-independent ASCII and on full internationalization, and says UTF-8 can be an upgrade path for ASCII-only protocols as long as its use is negotiated and a US-ASCII-compatible fallback such as UTF-7 is available.

The third is bi-directional text. The report says a consistent framework was needed but that no attempt was made to work on it.
sections.eli5: Some puzzles were too big for one weekend: how to write a name in any alphabet inside a web address, how to show writing that runs right to left, and how to pick the right look for letters shared by several languages.

sections.title: Recommendations and Conclusions
sections.content:
The recommendations to the IAB include examining existing RFCs for how they handle character sets, registering UTF-8 as a Character Encoding Scheme for MIME, developing IANA procedures for registering new character sets, encouraging an IRTF research group, and asking that application protocol RFCs include a section on 'multilingual Considerations'. It also states that full ISO 10646 is sufficient for use in Internet protocols, without excluding existing alternatives, and that no specific character set standard needs to be developed for the Internet.

For new protocols, the report says they SHOULD use ISO 10646 as the base charset unless there is an overriding reason, SHOULD use IANA registry values for parameters, and SHOULD tag text streams with the language of the text. For registering new character sets, a definition table must give each character's ISO 10646 code value, or a construction from combining characters, or a textual description. A character encoding scheme must define an algorithm taking any octet sequence to code values or to an 'illegal octet sequence' error.

The report says there are no security considerations associated with character sets. Its conclusion is that the framework should provide a foundation for interoperability, with open issues still to address.
sections.eli5: The grown-ups who ran the workshop ended with a to-do list: use the big shared alphabet in new things, always label your text, and write down clearly how each alphabet works before adding it to the list.
